title: How Insulin Lowers Blood Sugar
learningObjectives: Describe where insulin is made and what triggers its release
Explain how insulin lowers blood glucose in muscle, fat and liver, and how glucagon opposes it
Recognize expected findings of hypoglycemia in a client receiving insulin

claims.text: After a meal, blood glucose rises, and the body keeps blood glucose within a narrow range. (Sources differ on the upper limit, 100 vs 110 mg/dL, so no number is stated.)
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas, Figure 17.19

claims.text: Insulin is produced by beta cells in the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans).
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

claims.text: Elevated blood glucose stimulates beta cells to release insulin.
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

claims.text: Skeletal muscle and adipose cells are insulin's primary targets for glucose uptake.
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

claims.text: Insulin binds a tyrosine kinase receptor on the cell surface, which moves intracellular vesicles of GLUT4 glucose transporters to the plasma membrane, increasing glucose uptake.
claims.source: StatPearls, Biochemistry, Insulin Metabolic Effects (NBK525983); OpenStax A&P 2e, §17.9

claims.text: Glucose taken into cells is used for energy (glycolysis) or stored, so blood glucose falls.
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

claims.text: In the liver, insulin promotes conversion of glucose to glycogen and inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
claims.source: OpenStax A&P 2e, §17.9; StatPearls, Biochemistry, Insulin Metabolic Effects (NBK525983)

claims.text: Alpha cells release glucagon when blood glucose is low; glucagon stimulates the liver to break down glycogen and make glucose, raising blood glucose.
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

claims.text: As blood glucose falls, further insulin release is inhibited (negative feedback).
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas

claims.text: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which beta cells are destroyed and do not produce insulin.
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas (Diabetes Mellitus)

claims.text: In type 2 diabetes, cells become resistant to insulin and beta cells eventually become exhausted.
claims.source: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, §17.9 The Endocrine Pancreas (Diabetes Mellitus)

claims.text: Too much insulin in the bloodstream, or insulin without enough food, can cause low blood sugar; below 70 mg/dL is considered low.
claims.source: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, Low blood sugar (000386): Causes; ADA Standards of Care, Section 6, hypoglycemia level 1 <70 mg/dL

claims.text: Symptoms of low blood sugar include shaking or trembling, sweating, fast or pounding heartbeat, hunger and unclear thinking.
claims.source: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, Low blood sugar (000386): Symptoms

claims.text: Hot, dry, flushed skin, Kussmaul breathing, and increased thirst and urination point to hyperglycemia or DKA, not hypoglycemia (quiz distractors).
claims.source: Hinkle & Cheever, Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, Diabetes: hyperglycemia, DKA and hypoglycemia manifestations

scenes.narration: After a meal, **sugar** floods your blood. Yet blood glucose stays in a narrow range. The hormone that brings it down is **insulin**. Here's how.
Insulin is made in your ==pancreas==, by **beta cells** clustered in tiny islands called ==islets of Langerhans==. When blood glucose rises after you eat, beta cells release insulin into the blood.

Insulin travels to its main targets: ==skeletal muscle== and ==fat cells==. It binds a ==receptor== on the cell surface, which signals the cell to move **GLUT4** glucose transporters up to the membrane.
Those transporters open the door. Glucose flows out of the blood and into the cell, where it's burned for energy or stored. Blood glucose starts to fall.
In the ==liver==, insulin works differently. It tells liver cells to store glucose as **glycogen**, and it shuts down the liver's own glucose production, so less new sugar enters the blood.

params.definition: Insulin makes the liver store glucose and stop releasing it.

scenes.narration: Insulin has a partner. When glucose drops too low, **alpha cells** release ==glucagon==, which tells the liver to release glucose. And as glucose falls, insulin release slows. This **negative feedback** keeps you in balance.

When this fails, you get ==diabetes==. In **type 1**, the immune system destroys beta cells, so there's no insulin. In **type 2**, cells resist insulin and beta cells wear out. Either way, glucose stays high.

Quick NCLEX check. A client received insulin, then skipped lunch. Which finding should the nurse expect? [pause 2.5] The answer is C. Insulin kept moving glucose into cells with no food coming in, so glucose fell too low. Shakiness and sweating signal **hypoglycemia**.

params.question: A client received insulin, then skipped lunch. Which finding should the nurse expect?
params.rationale: Insulin + no food → glucose < 70 mg/dL: tremor, sweating, fast heartbeat.

scenes.narration: So: beta cells release **insulin** when glucose rises, muscle and fat take glucose in, and the liver stores it as **glycogen**. Follow for more A and P.

points: Beta cells release insulin when glucose rises
GLUT4 lets glucose into muscle and fat
Liver stores glucose; glucagon does the opposite
